title: Linear Transformations
bigIdea: A linear transformation is a rule for moving vectors that is completely determined by where it sends a basis: matrix columns record those moves, composition chains them, the determinant measures signed area scaling, and eigenvectors reveal directions that keep their heading.

concepts.title: A grid can move as one coherent object
concepts.summary: A linear transformation moves every point by a rule that preserves the origin and straight-line combinations. On a grid it can stretch, rotate, shear, or flatten the plane while keeping parallel lines parallel.
concepts.intuition: Imagine a transparent rubber grid whose arrows all move consistently: the origin stays put and every parallelogram remains a parallelogram.
misconceptions: A linear transformation can move the origin anywhere as long as the picture still looks smooth.
Every visually simple deformation is linear, including a translation or a bend.
A grid line has to remain the same length for the transformation to be linear.
visualHooks: A square grid stretches into a slanted parallelogram one point at a time.
Colored rubber bands show that parallel lines stay parallel while spacing changes.
A tiny creature watches the origin stay pinned while the rest of its world squishes.

concepts.title: Vectors are reusable moves
concepts.summary: A vector records a displacement with direction and magnitude, independent of where its arrow is drawn. Vectors add by head-to-tail motion and scale by changing how far the move goes.
concepts.intuition: A vector is an instruction to move: direction and amount, independent of where you draw its arrow.
misconceptions: A vector is a point whose coordinates identify its location.
Two arrows are different vectors whenever they start at different places.
Adding vectors means adding their lengths instead of adding horizontal and vertical moves.
visualHooks: Slide identical arrows across the plane and show that their displacement does not change.
Place two colored arrows head-to-tail so their sum appears as the shortcut arrow.
Stretch one arrow with a slider and watch every copy stretch by the same factor.

concepts.title: A basis is a pair of coordinate directions
concepts.summary: Two independent vectors form a basis for the plane when every vector can be made from exactly one combination of them. The coefficients are coordinates in that chosen basis.
concepts.intuition: A basis is a pair of reusable moves that lets you describe any point by how much of each move you take.
misconceptions: Only the horizontal and vertical unit vectors can be a basis.
A basis vector must have length one or be perpendicular to the other basis vector.
If a vector has two coordinates, those numbers mean the same thing in every basis.
visualHooks: Build a point by taking colored steps along two oblique basis arrows.
Show a square lattice becoming a slanted parallelogram lattice under a new basis.
Fade between the same geometric arrow and its changing coordinate labels.

concepts.title: Linearity preserves combinations
concepts.summary: A map T is linear when T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cu)=cT(u). Together these rules mean T sends every linear combination to the same combination of the transformed ingredients.
concepts.intuition: A linear map transforms a whole plane once you know how it transforms sums and scalings.
misconceptions: A map is linear whenever its graph is a straight line in a plot.
Preserving addition alone is enough; scaling may follow a different rule.
A linear map must preserve lengths, angles, or areas.
visualHooks: Compare transforming a sum before versus after splitting it into two arrows.
Animate a grid point as a weighted combination of two basis arrows.
Use a rubber sheet to show straight segments remain straight while lengths change.

concepts.title: Matrix columns are transformed basis vectors
concepts.summary: Once input and output bases are chosen, a linear map is encoded by a matrix. In the standard basis, the first column is T(i) and the second column is T(j), so matrix multiplication computes transformed coordinates.
concepts.intuition: A matrix is a compact record of where the basis arrows go: its columns are those transformed basis vectors.
misconceptions: The rows, rather than the columns, are always the images of the input basis vectors.
A matrix entry is a fixed physical length instead of a coordinate in the output basis.
The same matrix describes a map even after changing either the input or output basis.
visualHooks: Color the i and j arrows to match the first and second matrix columns.
Transform a unit square into a parallelogram and read its two edge vectors as columns.
Expand a coordinate combination and let the two columns assemble the result.

concepts.title: Composition chains transformations
concepts.summary: Applying one linear map after another gives a new linear map. For matrices, AB means B acts first and A acts second, which is why matrix multiplication is ordered and usually noncommutative.
concepts.intuition: Composition is stacking coordinate machines; the right-hand map acts first.
misconceptions: AB means A acts first because A is written first.
Matrix multiplication is entry-by-entry multiplication.
Every pair of matrices can be composed in either order with the same result.
visualHooks: Send a grid through a blue machine and then a gold machine, preserving the intermediate state.
Show the columns of AB as A acting on the columns of B.
Run AB and BA side by side so a shear and a stretch visibly disagree.

concepts.title: The determinant measures signed area scaling
concepts.summary: For a 2×2 matrix, the determinant is ad−bc. It is the signed area of the image of the unit square: its magnitude is the area scale and its sign records orientation reversal.
concepts.intuition: The determinant is the signed area of the image of a unit square.
misconceptions: The determinant is the area of the matrix's four entries.
A negative determinant means the map shrinks every vector.
A determinant of zero means only that one particular square landed on a line.
visualHooks: Fill the unit square, transform its corners, and track the signed parallelogram area.
Flip the plane through a mirror-like map and show the determinant sign change.
Flatten a square into a line while the area readout falls continuously to zero.

concepts.title: An inverse map rewinds the motion
concepts.summary: A linear map has an inverse exactly when its determinant is nonzero. The inverse sends every output back to its unique input, and composing a map with its inverse gives the identity transformation.
concepts.intuition: An inverse is a map that rewinds every arrow, so doing both returns each point exactly.
misconceptions: The inverse matrix is made by taking the reciprocal of every entry.
Any map can be undone even after it has flattened a plane into a line.
The inverse transformation is the same as reflecting the picture across a diagonal.
visualHooks: Play a grid forward through A and backward through A⁻¹ until every line returns home.
Contrast a reversible parallelogram map with a flattened map that has lost information.
Show AA⁻¹ as two stacked machines collapsing to an unchanged grid.

concepts.title: Eigenvectors keep their direction
concepts.summary: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose direction is unchanged by a map: Av=λv. The eigenvalue λ tells whether that direction stretches, shrinks, or flips, and some real matrices have no real eigenvectors.
concepts.intuition: An eigenvector is a special direction that survives the transformation without turning; its eigenvalue says stretch or flip.
misconceptions: An eigenvector is a point that stays fixed in place.
Every nonzero vector is an eigenvector of every matrix after choosing a suitable eigenvalue.
An eigenvalue must be positive because it measures a length.
visualHooks: Sweep many arrows through a shear and highlight the one line that does not rotate.
Show λ as a slider that stretches an eigenvector while its ray stays on one line.
Use the characteristic equation to turn a matrix question into an intersection of directions.

concepts.title: Changing basis changes the coordinates, not the vector
concepts.summary: A geometric vector is independent of coordinates, but its coordinate column changes with the chosen basis. Basis-change matrices translate between coordinate descriptions, and a map's matrix changes by conjugation when the same basis is used on input and output.
concepts.intuition: Changing basis is changing the measuring sticks: the arrow stays in the plane while its coordinate recipe changes.
misconceptions: Changing basis physically moves the vector in the plane.
The coordinate numbers of a vector are intrinsic and cannot depend on a basis.
A basis-change matrix can be applied without tracking which direction converts to which.
visualHooks: Hold one arrow still while two coordinate grids rotate and report different coefficients.
Use a conversion machine and its inverse to translate old coordinates into new ones.
Show P⁻¹AP as the same geometric action written from a new viewpoint.
